messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 39

He is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working as a bomb disposal technician, a job that has trained him to move carefully toward danger without showing fear. He speaks about his work with a kind of quiet pride, as someone who has made a career out of staying calm under pressure. When he first comes in, he appears composed, even reserved, and he tends to answer in practical terms. Over time, though, it becomes clear that the event that has unsettled him most was not something he confronted in the field, but what happened when his child became critically ill.

Before that illness, he describes himself as steady, disciplined, and hard to rattle. At work, he is used to weighing risks, checking procedures, and trusting his training. At home, he was the dependable one as well: the father who fixed what was broken, who handled crises without drama, who reassured his wife and children by staying level-headed. He and his wife had built a quiet life together, and their child had been at the center of that life, bringing the ordinary happiness that made his long hours and dangerous work feel worthwhile.

The change begins suddenly when his child falls seriously ill. He remembers the early signs in fragments: a fever that does not settle, the growing worry in his wife’s face, the medical appointments that become more frequent and more urgent. As the situation escalates, he finds himself in a place that feels alien to him. In emergencies at work, he knows the protocols. In the hospital, he feels stripped of that competence. He sits beside his child’s bed and watches monitors he cannot control. He listens to doctors speak in careful, measured language while he searches their faces for certainty. He says that the worst part is not the noise or the machinery, but the helplessness. There is no manual for standing by while a child’s life hangs in the balance.

During those days, he does what he has always done under stress: he shuts down his feelings long enough to get through the next task. He fills out forms, speaks with staff, calls relatives, and manages practical details while his wife cries in the bathroom or dozes in the chair. He becomes hyperalert to every change in his child’s breathing, every shift in tone from a nurse, every pause before a doctor answers a question. At night, he cannot sleep properly. He lies in the hospital chair with his clothes on, staring at the ceiling and replaying conversations, trying to predict the next bad turn. He feels guilt for not noticing something sooner, even when there was nothing obvious to notice, and he begins to blame himself for not being able to protect his child.

When his child survives, there is relief, but it does not arrive cleanly. He expects to feel only gratitude, yet he remains tense, as if his body has not received the message that the danger has passed. Back at home, ordinary sounds startle him. A phone ringing unexpectedly makes his heart jump. He is drawn to check on his child repeatedly, listening for breathing at night, pausing outside the bedroom door. He has trouble concentrating at work, even though he knows his tasks by heart. On jobs, he notices that his mind drifts to the hospital at moments when he needs to stay focused. He finds himself scanning for disaster in places where he once trusted routine.

He avoids reminders of the illness whenever he can. He does not like talking about the hospital stay, and when family members bring up that period, he changes the subject or leaves the room. He cannot look through old photos from those weeks. Certain hospital smells, the beeping of monitors on television, even the sight of medical gloves can bring back a wave of dread. In those moments, his chest tightens and he feels again that same powerless panic he felt at the bedside. He says that the memory comes back not as a story but as a sensation, with the same fear and the same sense of being trapped.

Over time, he becomes more distant from people outside the family. He remains devoted to his wife and child, but he is less easygoing than before and more easily irritated by small disruptions. He calls himself “not himself,” though he does not elaborate at first. Beneath that phrase is a man who has spent a lifetime believing that vigilance and skill can keep catastrophe contained, now finding that the thing that changed him happened in a place where control mattered least. Even now, he moves through his days with discipline, but there is a watchfulness in him that never fully settles, as if part of him is still standing guard beside a hospital bed.
